title: Programming Paradigms
body:
COMP 3649 introduces programming paradigms other than the imperative one every earlier course
used. The main focus is functional programming. The course opens with the [[Lambda Calculus]],
a model of computation whose only constructs are function definition and function application,
then moves to [[Haskell]], which adds data types and a compiler to that model.

In a functional language every computation is a function applied to arguments. Loops and
mutable variables do not exist, so repetition is written with [[Recursion]], and a value that
would have been updated in place becomes an argument passed forward to the next call. The
course finishes on [[Monad|monads]], which are how a language with no assignment still reads a
file and prints to a screen.

[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] proves that the lambda calculus and the [[Turing Machine]]
compute the same class of functions. A paradigm therefore determines how a program is written
and what a compiler can check about it before it runs. [[C]] in
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] and [[Java]] in [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] differ in
syntax while sharing one execution model, where statements run in sequence and overwrite
stored values as they go. Haskell has no statement and no assignment, and this course is the
extended answer to what programming looks like without them.

## Topics

### Two senses of the word paradigm

[[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] uses [[Paradigms]] for a way of decomposing a system
during [[Design]], where the [[Structured Approach]] splits a program by function and the
[[Object Oriented Approach]] splits it by thing. This course uses the word for the model a
language is built on. The two are independent axes: object oriented designs can be written in
C with structs and function pointers, and plenty of Java is structured code with a class
wrapped around it to satisfy the compiler.

### The lambda calculus

[[Lambda Calculus]] builds every program from two operations. Abstraction, written
$\lambda x. M$, defines a function of one parameter with body $M$. Application, written
$M\ N$, supplies an argument to a function. Computation is a single rewrite rule, beta
reduction, which substitutes the argument for the parameter throughout the body:

$$
(\lambda x.\ x + x)\ 3 \;\to\; 3 + 3 \;\to\; 6
$$

Numbers, booleans, pairs and recursion are all encoded from those two operations, which is
what makes the calculus Turing complete with no built-in data of any kind. A Church numeral
encodes $n$ as a function that applies another function $n$ times, so $2$ becomes
$\lambda f. \lambda x.\ f (f\ x)$, and arithmetic becomes composition. The Y combinator
recovers recursion for a function that has no name to call itself by.

Currying survives from the calculus into Haskell unchanged. Every function takes exactly one
argument, so `f x y` parses as `(f x) y`, and supplying fewer arguments than the definition
names returns a function waiting for the rest:

```haskell
add :: Int -> Int -> Int          -- really Int -> (Int -> Int)
add x y = x + y

add5 = add 5                      -- a function, not an error
add5 10                           -- 15
map (* 2) [1, 2, 3]               -- [2, 4, 6], no lambda needed
```

[[Partial Application]] covers the consequences.

### Haskell, and what purity means

| Property | Note | What it gives the compiler |
|---|---|---|
| Pure | [[Pure Function]] | an expression can be replaced by its value, so reordering, caching and parallel evaluation are all safe |
| Lazy | [[Lazy Evaluation]] | nothing is computed until another computation demands it |
| Statically typed | [[Static Typing]] | every type is checked before the program runs, with no cast available to bypass the check |

A [[Pure Function]] returns the same result for the same arguments and changes nothing outside
itself. That is a stronger promise than it sounds, because it means an expression can be
replaced by its value anywhere it appears, which is referential transparency and is what
licenses the compiler to reorder, cache or parallelise.

Purity makes laziness safe, because an expression with no effect can be evaluated at any point
without changing the result. The type system makes purity enforceable, because a function that
performs input or output has to declare it in its signature.

[[Immutability]] is the same idea stated about data. A name binds to one value for its whole
scope:

```haskell
x = 5
x = 6        -- compile error: Multiple declarations of 'x'
```

There is no assignment statement to write, so a variable never changes and a function cannot
alter what its caller passed in. Updating a structure builds a new value that shares its
unchanged parts with the old one, which is why persistent data structures cost less than
copying suggests.

### Repetition without a loop

A loop counter is a variable overwritten on every iteration, and Haskell has no such variable.
Repetition happens by [[Recursion]], and the counter becomes an argument each call passes
forward:

```haskell
mySum :: [Int] -> Int
mySum []     = 0                  -- base case: the empty list sums to 0
mySum (x:xs) = x + mySum xs       -- one element plus the sum of the rest

mySum [1, 2, 3]                   -- 6
```

The definition is two equations and the compiler picks by matching the shape of the argument,
which is pattern matching. `(x:xs)` splits a list into its first element and the remainder.

[[Recursion Schemes]] names the shapes this takes. Structural recursion follows the shape of
the data and terminates on any finite input, which is what licenses proof by induction over
it. Accumulator passing carries a running result forward as an extra argument. Folds abstract
both, so `foldr (+) 0` is `mySum` with the operation supplied by the caller, and most list
code is written with a fold and no explicit recursion.

[[List Comprehension]] is set-builder notation from [[Sets]] written with brackets:

```haskell
[x * x | x <- [1..10], even x]    -- [4, 16, 36, 64, 100]
```

It desugars into `map`, `filter` and `concatMap`. [[Recursive Backtracking]] puts the same
machinery to work on search problems, where generators supply the choices and guards prune
them. The imperative version of [[Backtracking]] spends most of its code undoing a partial
solution before trying the next branch, and nothing here is mutable, so there is no state to
undo.

### Types

[[Static Typing]] means every type is checked before the program runs. Haskell's version is
stronger than [[C]]'s because C permits a [[Type casting|cast]] around its own check, which
makes the guarantee advisory. [[Type Inference]] keeps full checking affordable to write: the
Hindley-Milner algorithm finds the principal type, the most general type an expression can
have, with no annotation from the programmer.

[[Algebraic Data Type]] is how a type is declared. A sum type is one of several alternatives,
written with `|`. A product type holds several fields at once. Both are taken apart by pattern
matching:

```haskell
data Shape = Circle Double | Rect Double Double   -- a sum of two products

area :: Shape -> Double
area (Circle r) = pi * r * r
area (Rect w h) = w * h
```

The compiler warns on any match that misses a case, so adding a constructor to a type produces
a work list of every place that needs updating, which is what makes a large refactor
tractable. The standard consequence is absence in the type itself:

```haskell
data Maybe a = Nothing | Just a

safeDiv :: Int -> Int -> Maybe Int
safeDiv _ 0 = Nothing
safeDiv x y = Just (x `div` y)
```

A caller of `safeDiv` cannot use the result without handling `Nothing`, because the type is
`Maybe Int` and unwrapping it requires matching both cases. Every other type is therefore
guaranteed to hold a value, which removes the null pointer as a category.

Two kinds of polymorphism share a word and nothing else. [[Parametric Polymorphism]] is one
implementation covering every type, and it cannot inspect the values it holds, which is where
its guarantees come from: a function typed `a -> a` has no possible definition except the
identity, because it knows nothing about `a` that would let it do anything else.
[[Polymorphism]] in COMP 2633 is many implementations selected at run time by an object's
class. [[Type Class]] is a third kind, supplying different code per type, retrofittable onto a
type from a library you do not control, and able to dispatch on the return type in a way no
[[Interface]] can.

### Lazy evaluation

Nothing is computed until it is demanded. That makes an infinite structure an ordinary value:

```haskell
naturals = [1..]                  -- an infinite list
take 5 naturals                   -- [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
take 3 (filter even [1..])        -- [2, 4, 6], stops after finding three
```

`head (filter p xs)` stops at the first match with no break statement, and `if` and `&&` are
ordinary functions with no special syntax, since an argument that is never demanded is never
evaluated. The costs are space leaks, where unevaluated expressions pile up holding memory,
and a cost analysis that depends on what the consumer of a value demands from it.

### Monads

The type class ladder [[Functor]] to `Applicative` to [[Monad]] answers three progressively
harder questions about applying a function to a value that sits inside a structure. Only the
top rung lets a later step depend on the value an earlier step produced.

The problem is concrete. Chaining three operations that each return `Maybe` means unwrapping
and rewrapping at every step:

```haskell
-- without a monad
case safeDiv 100 5 of
    Nothing -> Nothing
    Just a  -> case safeDiv a 0 of
        Nothing -> Nothing
        Just b  -> Just (a + b)

-- with do notation, which is sugar for >>=
calc = do
    a <- safeDiv 100 5            -- a is 20
    b <- safeDiv a 0              -- Nothing, so the whole block is Nothing
    return (a + b)
```

[[Monad]] is `return` and `>>=` obeying the two identity laws and associativity, with
`x <- e` desugaring to `e >>= \x ->`. The failure propagation in the second version is
supplied by `Maybe`'s definition of `>>=` and appears nowhere in the code. `Maybe`, `Either`,
lists, `State` and `IO` all implement that one interface over completely unrelated internals,
which is why one notation covers failure, state and input.

### Effects

[[Monadic IO]] is how a pure language performs effects. A value of type `IO a` is a
description of an action, so constructing one is pure and the runtime executes only the
description that `main` evaluates to.

```haskell
main :: IO ()
main = do
    name <- getLine
    putStrLn ("hello " ++ name)
```

The type system provides no function `IO a -> a`, so an effect cannot be smuggled into pure
code. A function typed `Int -> Int` therefore provably performed no input or output, which is
the strongest single claim Haskell's types make and the reason a signature carries so much
information.

### Nondeterminism

[[Nondeterminism]] arrives from [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]]. Its two readings, guess the
right branch and explore every branch, are the specification that the list monad implements:

```haskell
pairs = do
    x <- [1, 2]
    y <- "ab"
    return (x, y)
-- [(1,'a'), (1,'b'), (2,'a'), (2,'b')]
```

Each `<-` chooses from a list and the result collects every combination, because the list
monad's `>>=` is `concatMap`. The [[NFA]] acceptance rule, where a string is accepted if any
path accepts it, is the same idea one level of abstraction lower. A [[Pure Function]] is
deterministic by construction, so nondeterminism here is a data structure a program opts into.

### Correctness and category theory

[[Program Correctness]] is what purity is for. In a pure language `=` means equality, so equals
can be substituted for equals and a program can be transformed by algebra. Proving
`mySum (xs ++ ys) = mySum xs + mySum ys` is two cases and an induction hypothesis, with no
reasoning about state at any point. [[Algebraic Data Type]] supplies the case split, and
structural induction is [[Proof By Induction]] with $\mathbb{N}$ replaced by a recursive type,
proving a property for a constructor's arguments and then for the constructor. [[Induction]] in
[[DISCRETE MATH]] is the same technique on numbers.

[[Category Theory]] is where the definition of a monad comes from, and the course goes far
enough in to derive it. Objects and arrows give composition and identity, a functor is a
mapping that preserves both, a natural transformation maps between functors, and a monad is an
endofunctor carrying $\eta$ (`return`) and $\mu$ (`join`) that satisfy the monoid axioms. Bind
is then map followed by flatten, `m >>= f = join (fmap f m)`. Naturality turns out to be
parametricity: a function typed `forall a. F a -> G a` cannot inspect its elements, so it
commutes with `fmap` automatically.

### The other paradigms

| | Imperative and procedural | Object oriented | Functional | Declarative |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A program is | a sequence of commands | objects sending messages | expressions being evaluated | a description of the answer |
| The unit is | the procedure | the [[Classes\|class]] | the [[Function\|function]] | the rule or the query |
| State | global and mutable | partitioned, owned by an [[Object]] | replaced by values | not exposed |
| Repetition by | the loop | the loop | [[Recursion Schemes\|recursion]] | recursion or set operations |
| Formal model | [[Turing Machine]] | Turing machine with access control | [[Lambda Calculus]] | logic and relations |
| In the vault | [[C]], [[Assembly]] | [[Java]], [[Classes]] | [[Haskell]] | [[SQL]], [[React]], [[Regular Expressions]] |

Imperative programming matches what the hardware executes. A list of commands that change
memory is an [[Instructions|instruction stream]] with named variables and structured control
flow on top of it. Procedural programming adds the [[Subroutines|subroutine]] and with it the
call stack, which is where local [[Variable Scope|scope]], automatic lifetimes and recursion
come from. Object orientation keeps that execution model and fences the mutable state off one
object at a time, which is [[Encapsulation]]. Functional programming addresses the same problem
with shared mutable state by removing the mutation, so the two answers differ in whether they
restrict who may write or delete the write itself.

Declarative languages describe the result and let an implementation choose the algorithm.
[[SQL]]'s planner picks the join order, [[React]] diffs a described tree against the DOM, and a
[[Regular Expressions|regex]] describes a set of [[Strings]] that something else compiles into
an [[NFA]]. A [[List Comprehension]] is declarative in this sense while a fold is not. Logic
programming is the fifth paradigm, and its execution model is backtracking search plus
unification, the same unification Hindley-Milner runs over types.

### These features outside Haskell

The functional features reached the mainstream through JavaScript, so most of
[[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] is recognisable from this course.

| Feature | Origin in the calculus | Where it was already seen |
|---|---|---|
| functions are values | an abstraction is a term like any other | [[JS Functions]], where functions are [[Objects]] |
| higher-order functions | application where the function is a parameter | [[Call Back Function]], `setTimeout` |
| anonymous functions | lambda terms never needed names | [[Anonymous Function]], [[Arrow Syntax]] |
| closures | a term keeps its free variables bound | [[Closure]] |
| `map`, `filter`, `reduce` | folds over a structure | [[Array Functions]] |
| currying | one argument at a time | [[Partial Application]] |
| recursion with no loop | the Y combinator | [[Recursion]], [[Recursion Schemes]] |
| immutable state | values replace variables | [[React]]'s rule against mutating state directly |

JavaScript offers these features and permits the alternative. Haskell removes the alternative,
which is what turns each one into a guarantee the compiler can rely on.

### Concurrency, where the choice pays

[[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] spends most of its synchronisation material on shared mutable state. A
[[Critical Section]] needs a [[Mutex Lock]] or a [[Semaphores|semaphore]] around it,
[[Spin Lock]] and [[Synchronization]] cover the variants, and every missing lock is a race
condition that appears on some runs and not others. [[Message Passing]] avoids the shared data
by copying, at the cost of a hand-designed protocol.

A race condition requires two things: data reachable by more than one [[Thread]] and at least
one writer. [[Immutability]] removes the writer, so a program with no mutable [[Shared Memory]]
cannot express a race at all. This is the most practical argument the paradigm makes, and it is
why [[Pure Function]] and [[Immutability]] are the two notes to read first.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] (COMP 2613) is the theoretical prerequisite.
  [[Lambda Calculus]] originates there, [[Turing Machine]] is the imperative counterpart,
  [[Undecidability]] limits every paradigm equally, and the [[NFA]] is [[Nondeterminism]]
  made concrete.
- [[DISCRETE MATH]] (MATH 1271) supplies [[Proof By Induction]] and [[Induction]], which
  become structural induction in [[Program Correctness]], and [[Sets]], whose notation
  [[List Comprehension]] borrows.
- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101) is where [[Group]], [[Homomorphism]] and
  [[Isomorphism]] establish the structure-preserving map that [[Category Theory]]
  generalises. The monoid axioms are the [[Monad]] laws.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] (COMP 1633) owns [[Recursion]] and what a stack
  frame costs. [[C]], [[Variable]] and [[Structure]] are the mutable-state comparison used
  throughout.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] (COMP 2633) holds the design sense of
  [[Paradigms]] and the run-time sense of [[Polymorphism]].
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) has [[Java]] and the [[Abstract Data Type]], which
  separates interface from implementation by a different mechanism than [[Type Class]].
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655) has [[Assembly]] and [[Subroutines]], the paradigm
  every other one compiles down to, and settles the tail-call question in
  [[Recursion Schemes]].
- [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] (COMP 3612) is where these features were already in use, in
  [[JS Functions]], [[Closure]], [[Array Functions]] and [[React]].
- [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] (COMP 3659) supplies [[Concurrency]], [[Thread]] and the locks that
  shared mutable state requires.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] applies recursive thinking in [[Backtracking]] and
  [[Dynamic Programming]], and its [[Time Complexity]] analysis is what
  [[Lazy Evaluation]] complicates.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] covers [[Simulation]] and the [[Chomsky Hierarchy]].
